### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to efficiently compute the optimal acceptance rate for MDSD under large vocabulary sizes (thousands of tokens) to quantify the gap between existing verification algorithms and theoretical upper bounds. None of the prior papers explicitly address this purpose. While many papers (e.g., [1], [2], [3], [4], [6], [15], [16]) focus on speculative decoding and its efficiency, they do not aim to compute the optimal acceptance rate or quantify the gap between practical algorithms and theoretical limits. This specific objective is absent from prior work.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves taking the dual of the optimal transport problem, leveraging the total unimodularity (TUM) of the coefficient matrix to transform the computation of the optimal acceptance rate into a subset selection problem, and designing efficient solvers using the convexity structure of set functions for specific draft distributions (with or without replacement). Paper [6] discusses speculative decoding using optimal transport but does not leverage TUM or transform the problem into subset selection. Papers [9], [10], [11], [13], and [18] discuss optimal transport methods, but none combine TUM with subset selection or address the specific draft distribution structure. Papers [12], [14], [17], [18], and [21] discuss TUM in optimization problems, but they do not apply it to speculative decoding or optimal transport in this manner. Thus, the mechanism is novel.

### Evaluation
The evaluation facet involves providing a practical method to compute the theoretical acceptance rate upper bound for given draft distributions, demonstrating scalability to large vocabularies (thousands of tokens), and comparing against LP solvers that are limited to toy models. Papers [6], [15], and [16] discuss speculative decoding efficiency and acceptance rates but do not provide a method to compute theoretical upper bounds or scale to large vocabularies. While [6] uses optimal transport, its evaluation design does not match the contribution's focus on theoretical bounds or scalability. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design, making this facet novel.

### Domain
The domain is speculative decoding for accelerating large language model inference. Many prior papers ([1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [15], [16], [19], [20]) work in this application area, even if they target different sub-problems or datasets. Therefore, the domain is covered.
